explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, Joseph asks for the body of Jesus. He goes to Pilate, the governor, and makes the request himself (Matthew 27:58). That takes some nerve, and I think it took a lot of love too. Pilate orders that the body be given to him.

Not the garments, friend. Joseph asks for something much more personal: the body of Jesus (Matthew 27:58). I'll admit I've asked for the wrong thing at the counter before, but Joseph knows exactly what he's after. Pilate orders that it be given to him.
Not the cross, baker. Joseph isn't after the wood, he asks Pilate for the body of Jesus (Matthew 27:58). Picture walking up to the governor and asking for THAT. Pilate orders that it be given to him.
True, baker. Joseph takes the body and wraps it in a clean linen cloth (Matthew 27:59). The text gives us that detail right there, clean linen. I think that says Joseph handled the body with care.
It's actually true, friend. The text says Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen cloth (Matthew 27:59). Clean is the word the text uses. I think Joseph was careful about it.
Right, baker, it's Joseph's own new tomb, the one cut into the rock (Matthew 27:60). Think about that. A rich man lays Jesus' body in a new tomb that's his own. I think that says a lot about Joseph.

Not Pilate's, friend. Pilate only gave the order for the body to be given to Joseph (Matthew 27:58). The tomb belongs to Joseph. The text says it's his own new tomb that he had cut into the rock (Matthew 27:60).
Not the priests', baker. They don't show up until the next day (Matthew 27:62). Joseph puts the body in his own new tomb that he had cut into the rock (Matthew 27:60). Nobody had to lend him a thing.
Yes, baker, a great stone. Joseph rolls it across the entrance and goes away (Matthew 27:60). The text calls it great, and I'd guess he needed a good push. Nobody rolls a great stone by accident.
Close, but not a log, friend. The text says Joseph rolled a great stone across the entrance to the tomb (Matthew 27:60). A log would be a pretty sad door. A stone is what the text gives us.

Not a cart, baker. Imagine a cart parked at the entrance with a sticky note on it: "Back in five minutes." The text says Joseph rolled a great stone across the entrance and went away (Matthew 27:60). A stone, not a cart.

explanations.answer: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary are sitting there opposite the tomb (Matthew 27:61). Joseph has gone away, but they stay. I think they're not ready to leave yet.

Good guess, friend, but not those sisters. Matthew names Mary Magdalene and the other Mary (Matthew 27:61). Two Marys is easy to mix up, like grabbing the wrong cookie tin. These two are sitting opposite the tomb.

Not these two, baker. Elizabeth, John the Baptist's mother (Luke 1:57-60), and Anna the prophetess (Luke 2:36) belong to the stories of Jesus' birth. At the tomb it's Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, sitting opposite it (Matthew 27:61).

explanations.answer: After three days I will rise again
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The chief priests and Pharisees say, "we remember that while He was alive that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will rise again.’" (Matthew 27:63) They call Him a deceiver, but they remember His words. That's what they bring to Pilate.

explanations.answer: I will come down from the cross
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. Those words were said by others, who said, "…let Him come down now from the cross…" (Matthew 27:42). What the priests and Pharisees remember is, "After three days I will rise again." (Matthew 27:63)

explanations.answer: Elijah will come to save Me
explanations.explanation: Not that, baker. Elijah comes up when someone near the cross says, "Let us see if Elijah comes to save Him." (Matthew 27:49) That's what that person said, not what the priests and Pharisees remember. They remember Jesus saying, "After three days I will rise again." (Matthew 27:63)

Yes, baker. They say, "Otherwise, His disciples may come and steal Him away and tell the people He has risen from the dead." (Matthew 27:64) That's their worry, spelled out. They want the tomb secured until the third day.

explanations.answer: The crowds riot at the tomb
explanations.explanation: Not a riot, friend. The text never mentions the crowds there. The fear they name is, "…His disciples may come and steal Him away…" (Matthew 27:64). That's the worry they bring to Pilate.

Not Joseph, baker. They never mention him at all. Their worry is that "…His disciples may come and steal Him away and tell the people He has risen from the dead." (Matthew 27:64) That's the whole concern.

True, baker. Pilate says, "You have a guard…" and then, "Go, make the tomb as secure as you know how." (Matthew 27:65) He hands the job right back to them. I'd say that's a governor who is done with the whole conversation.
It's true, friend. Pilate tells them, "Go, make the tomb as secure as you know how." (Matthew 27:65) He doesn't argue and doesn't add a plan of his own. He just says go and do it.

That one's false, baker. They don't decide against a guard. The text says they went and secured the tomb by sealing the stone and posting the guard (Matthew 27:66). The guard is posted, the opposite of what this statement says.

Right, baker, it's false. The text says they secured the tomb by sealing the stone and posting the guard (Matthew 27:66). Pilate had said, "You have a guard…" and they used it (Matthew 27:65). A sealed stone and a guard, all on purpose.
